Ioana sees the flat she has rented in the centre of Lyon for the first time. Her neighbour, Madame Bernard, shows her around.
There’s a kitchen, a living room and two bedrooms.
Two bedrooms? That’s great! The kitchen is small, but the bedroom is big.
Do you have family in Romania?
Yes, my parents are in Iași and I have a brother.
He’s nineteen. He’s a student. And you, do you have children?
I have a daughter. She’s forty… and she has three children!
Three grandchildren! And you have a cat, don’t you?
Yes, Victor. He’s twelve. Do you have a cat too?
No, I don’t have a cat. I don’t have any pets.
Victor loves visits. He’ll often be at your place, be warned!

Liaison: a final consonant, normally silent, is pronounced when the next word starts with a vowel. “vous avez” = “voo-za-VAY”, “les enfants” = “lay-zã-FÃ”, “deux ans” = “duh-ZÃ”.
Elision: le, la, je, ne, de lose their vowel before another vowel and take an apostrophe: l’appartement, j’ai, n’ai, d’animal. It’s read as one chunk.
EU and ŒU are like the German “ö” or the vowel in “bird” with rounded lips. Deux = “duh”, sœur = “sur” (rounded).
CH is read like English “sh”: chat = “sha”, chambre = “shãbr”, chien = “shyẽ”.
ILLE after a vowel is read as a short “y”: famille = “fa-MEE-y”, fille = “fee-y”. Exception: ville = “veel”.
Watch the final consonant: six, huit, dix are “sees, weet, dees” on their own, but “see, wee, dee” before a consonant: six chats = “see sha”, and “seez” before a vowel: six ans = “see-ZÃ”.
AVOIR is the second most important verb after ÊTRE. Learn them together.
“Ils ont” (they have) and “ils sont” (they are) look alike! You can hear the difference: “eel-ZÕ” (ont, with a linking z) versus “eel SÕ” (sont, with an s). A very common mistake.
“Je” becomes “j’” before “ai”: never “je ai”. Likewise “il a” is simply read “ee-la”.
2. Age: with AVOIR, “I have thirty years”
Watch out, English speakers: French gives your age with “to have”, not “to be”. Always add the word “ans” (years).
How old are you? (word for word: “What age do you have?”)
The classic English-speaker mistake is “Je suis 30”. The correct form is “J’ai 30 ans”. And don’t forget “ans”: “J’ai trente” alone is incomplete.
3. Articles: un, une, des / le, la, les
In French almost every noun has an article in front of it, even where English has none: “J’aime les chats” = “I like cats”.
The plural adds -s, but you DON’T hear it: “chat” and “chats” are both read “sha”. You recognise the plural by the article: le / les, un / des.
Every noun has a gender, and it isn’t logical: “la chambre” (feminine), but “le salon” (masculine) and “la voiture” (the car, feminine). Learn every word WITH its article.
“Des” has no exact English equivalent: “J’ai des frères” = “I have (some) brothers”. Don’t leave it out.
4. “Il y a” = there is, there are
“Il y a” is a fixed phrase that says something exists somewhere. It doesn’t change in the plural.
What is it? What’s the matter?
Negative: “Il n’y a pas de…” = “There’s no… / there aren’t any…”: “Il n’y a pas de balcon.”
After a negation, un / une / des turn into DE (or d’ before a vowel).
The typical mistake: “Je n’ai pas un chat”. After “pas” comes “de”. Careful: le / la / les DON’T change: “Je n’aime pas le café.”
17 to 19 are easy: “ten-seven”, “ten-eight”, “ten-nine” (dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf). The big numbers, with their surprises (70 = “sixty-ten”!), come in chapter 4.
“Neuf” has a special form before “ans” and “heures”: “neuf ans” = “nuh-VÃ”.
